Chapter 10: Training the Unconscious—How to Make Better Snap Judgments
You know, it’s tempting to think of intuition as this mysterious gift—something you’re either born with or you’re not. But what if I told you that snap judgments can actually be trained? Our minds are always learning, always adapting. And with the right kind of practice, you can get a whole lot better at making quick, accurate decisions.
Picture a rookie firefighter, stepping into the chaos for the very first time. Every call feels overwhelming, and every decision is a struggle. But after a while—call after call, mistake after mistake—something shifts. Their instincts start to sharpen. Suddenly, the danger signs become clearer. Acting fast doesn’t seem so impossible anymore; it becomes almost automatic.
And here’s the thing—this isn’t just for the experts. Anyone can train their intuition. It doesn’t matter if you’re in an emergency room, a boardroom, or even just making quick calls at home. The secret? Practice. You need repeated exposure to situations where quick decisions matter. But just as important is feedback. When you see the results of your choices—both the wins and the misses—your mind starts to notice patterns. It learns what works, and what doesn’t. And little by little, your instincts get sharper.
Let me tell you about a hospital that wanted to step up its emergency care game. Instead of drowning in endless checklists and data, the staff zeroed in on just a handful of crucial indicators. They practiced making quick calls, learned from their stumbles, and over time, their intuition got better. The payoff? Better patient care, faster response times, and way fewer mistakes.
But there’s more to it than just repetition. The right environment makes all the difference. If you’re distracted, stressed, or weighed down by bias, your judgment gets cloudy. The best kind of training happens in a space that’s supportive, focused, and open to learning from both success and failure.
Most people don’t realize just how much they can improve their intuition. They write off quick thinking as something mysterious, unchangeable. But actually, our minds are pretty incredible at adapting. With enough effort, and a bit of patience, anyone can get better at snap judgments.
So, what’s the real challenge? It’s about seeking out chances to practice, inviting feedback, and sticking with it—even when it feels awkward or slow at first. You’re not aiming for perfection—just a little progress each time. And when you do that, you’ll notice your first impressions start to get clearer, more reliable, and a whole lot more useful.
